entries.title: BYTE
entries.body: A unit of computer data measurement equivalent to 8 bits. Each bit is a binary digit (`0` or `1`), which means that a byte can represent 256 (`2^8`) unique combinations.

entries.title: OAP - OPEN ASSETS PROTOCOL
entries.body: The Open Assets Protocol (OAP), designed by Flavien Charlon in 2013, represents the first functional implementation of Colored Coins. This protocol made it possible to store and transfer non-native assets on the Bitcoin blockchain, in the form of tokens called “Colored Coins”. These are specifically marked to symbolize a promise, whether formal or informal, of exchange for real goods or services.

entries.title: OBOE - OFF-BY-ONE ERROR
entries.body:
A logic error where a loop iterates one time too many or one too few, often due to incorrect use of comparison operators or wrong indices when handling data structures. Two notable instances of this bug exist in Bitcoin.

The more consequential one is found in the difficulty adjustment calculation. The algorithm measures the time elapsed during a period of 2016 blocks by comparing the timestamp of the first block of the period with that of the last, then compares this duration with the target time of `1\,209\,600` seconds (`2016 \times 600`). The problem is that the difference between the first and the last block of a period covers only 2015 block intervals, not 2016:
```math
T = t_{2015} - t_0
```
The intervals counted are:
```math
\underbrace{[t_0 \to t_1]}_{1},\ \underbrace{[t_1 \to t_2]}_{2},\ \ldots,\ \underbrace{[t_{2014} \to t_{2015}]}_{2015}
```
That is 2015 intervals. To obtain 2016, the last block of the previous period would have had to be used as the starting point:
```math
T_{correct}\ =\ t_{2015}\ -\ t_{-1}
```
Where `t_{-1}` denotes the timestamp of the last block of the previous period (block `n - 1` for a period that begins at block `n`). The algorithm therefore compares 2015 actual intervals with the theoretical time of 2016 intervals. This offset introduces a bias of approximately `\frac{1}{2016} \approx 0{,}05\,\%` toward a slightly overestimated difficulty.

The main consequence of this bug is that retarget periods do not overlap: the timestamp of the last block of one period does not enter into the calculation of the next period. This discontinuity makes the *time warp* attack possible, in which a majority attacker manipulates the timestamp of the last block of a period without it affecting the calculation of the following period. Truly fixing this bug would require a hard fork, but *time warp* attacks can be prevented through a simple soft fork by adding constraints on timestamps.

The second instance of an *off-by-one* bug in Bitcoin is the *dummy element* in `OP_CHECKMULTISIG`, where the opcode consumes an extra stack element by mistake. This bug was effectively fixed by BIP-0147 (*NULLDUMMY*), which requires this element to be a null value.

entries.title: OCEAN
entries.body: A Bitcoin mining pool launched in November 2023 by Luke Dashjr, a long-time developer of Bitcoin Core and Bitcoin Knots. Ocean stands out for its approach focused on decentralizing mining: miners can select or build their own block *templates*, which reduces dependence on centralized pool operators. The pool uses the TIDES payout system (*Transparent Index of Distinct Extended Shares*), which rewards miners directly through the outputs of *coinbase* transactions. The project continues the work of Eligius, the mining pool that Luke Dashjr had launched in 2011.

entries.title: OFF-CHAIN
entries.body: Refers to transactions or activities more or less related to Bitcoin that take place outside the main blockchain, but that have a link or anchor to it. They are not immediately recorded on the blockchain, but require additional mechanisms to ensure their security and finality. These operations are often justified by a desire to get around the technical limitations inherent to Bitcoin, in order to have transactions with fast finality, low fees, and more capacity or functionality.

entries.title: OFF-GRID
entries.body:
Refers to a Bitcoin mining operation that runs autonomously, without being connected to the main electrical grid. Off-grid miners generally use alternative energy sources such as solar, wind, or hydroelectric power, or generators running on fossil fuels (for example, gas intended for flaring). This model is often preferred to reduce energy costs, since it is partly based on energy that, without mining, would be wasted. Off-grid miners have the advantage of being able to set up in remote places, in order to consume this energy that is too far from populations. 

Off-grid mining often presents ecological advantages, because it can, in some cases, help reduce greenhouse gas emissions by limiting flaring. Moreover, it makes certain renewable energy production projects economically viable despite their natural intermittency.

entries.title: OFFER
entries.body: Within the framework of BOLT-12, “*offers*” are static QR codes for making multiple payments on the Lightning Network. Unlike classic invoices, *offers* can be reused. They make it possible to generate multiple invoice requests. When a user scans a QR code containing an *offer*, they send a message to request a new invoice from the associated Lightning node. The node responds with an invoice that the payer can use. *Offers* thus make it possible to have a single identifier to receive many payments from several different users on Lightning.

entries.title: OMNI
entries.body: Omni Layer (formerly Mastercoin) is an *open-source*, decentralized platform for creating and managing assets on the Bitcoin blockchain. Assets on Omni include Tether (USDT) and MaidSafeCoin (MAID).

entries.title: ON-CHAIN
entries.body: Refers to transactions recorded directly on the Bitcoin blockchain. This term is the opposite of “*off-chain*”, which refers to operations that are more or less linked with the Bitcoin blockchain, but that take place outside the main blockchain.

entries.title: ON-GRID
entries.body:
Refers to a Bitcoin mining operation that is connected to the general electrical grid. *On-grid* miners plug into the conventional electrical grid, also used by residential consumers, to power their ASICs. This method offers a stable energy source, but is often more expensive compared to *off-grid* mining, due to more limited negotiating margins.

Sometimes, *on-grid* mining farms participate in demand management programs. They adjust their energy consumption according to fluctuations in electricity production and consumption on the grid, in order to maintain balance and avoid waste or *blackouts*.

entries.title: ONION ADDRESS
entries.body:
A special address used to access an *onion service* on the Tor network. It ends with the suffix `.onion` and is not resolved by conventional DNS: only a client connected to the Tor network can reach it. A v3 onion address (the current format) is a string of 56 alphanumeric characters derived from the service's public key `Ed25519`, which allows the client to cryptographically verify that it is communicating with the right server.

In the Bitcoin ecosystem, onion addresses allow Bitcoin and Lightning nodes to expose their services without revealing their real IP address. A node configured with an address `.onion` remains reachable by its peers on the P2P network, while concealing its geographic location and the identity of its operator. This strengthens censorship resistance and privacy, at the cost of slightly higher latency than *clearnet*.

entries.title: ONION MESSAGE
entries.body:
Lightweight and flexible messages transmitted between peers on the Lightning Network using onion routing, without requiring the sending of funds or the locking of liquidity. Unlike Lightning payments that go through HTLCs, onion messages are simply relayed from peer to peer along existing connections, which makes them free for the sender.

Onion messages are the communication building block of the BOLT-12 protocol (*offers*). They allow a payer to contact a recipient to request an invoice, even without a direct channel between them. Thanks to *blinded paths*, the recipient can receive these messages without revealing their identity or their position in the network: they build an encrypted route to themselves from a popular node, which dilutes their identity among many possible candidates.

Beyond *offers*, onion messages pave the way for asynchronous payments: an LSP can hold a payment and use an onion message to signal that the recipient is online, thus eliminating the requirement for the receiver to be connected permanently.

entries.title: ONION SERVICE
entries.body:
A service hosted on the Tor network, accessible only via an `.onion` address, without exposing the server's IP address. Formerly called “*hidden service*”, the official term was renamed “*onion service*” by the Tor project. The server and the client communicate through Tor circuits, so that neither knows the IP address of its counterpart.

An onion service works by publishing introduction points (*introduction points*) in the Tor network's distributed hash table. The client then chooses a rendezvous point (*rendezvous point*) and communicates it to the service via an introduction point. The client and the server each build a Tor circuit to this rendezvous point, in order to establish a mutual connection without any data passing in the clear over the internet.

In the context of Bitcoin, many Bitcoin Core and Lightning nodes expose an onion service to accept incoming connections anonymously. This allows a node operator to participate in the P2P network without revealing their IP address or their location, which strengthens the censorship resistance and privacy of the infrastructure.

entries.title: ONION_PRIVATE_KEY
entries.body: A file formerly used in Bitcoin Core to store a private key associated with a Tor V2 hidden service for the `-listenonion` option. This file has no longer been used since version 0.21.0, in favor of Tor V3.

entries.title: ONION_V3_PRIVATE_KEY
entries.body: A file used in Bitcoin Core to store a private key associated with a Tor hidden service for the `-listenonion` option. When this option is enabled, `bitcoind` automatically creates a Tor hidden service, allowing the node to communicate on the Tor network.

entries.title: OOR PAYMENT
entries.body:
An instant payment mechanism within the Ark protocol that allows VTXOs to be transferred between users without waiting for the next round. Since Ark rounds are infrequent (15 to 60 minutes) and require liquidity from the ASP, OOR payments offer a fast and less costly alternative for everyday transfers.

To make an OOR payment, the sender creates a transaction reusing the forfeit clause (*forfeit clause*) of the VTXO's policy, which redirects it to a new VTXO belonging to the recipient. The ASP co-signs this transaction, then the sender passes it to the receiver. The resulting OOR VTXO has the same properties as a classic VTXO: it can be used as an input in a round or serve for a new OOR payment.

The trust model differs, however, from payments made in a round. The recipient of an OOR payment must trust the sender and the ASP not to collude to carry out a double spend. In case of fraud, the signatures of both spends become public, allowing the receiver to cryptographically prove the violation. The user can at any time submit their OOR VTXO in the next round to refresh it into a fully *trustless* classic VTXO.

OOR Payments are sometimes referred to by the term “*arkoor*”.

entries.title: OP_0 - 0X00
entries.body:
Pushes the value 0 onto the stack. It is often used to represent the boolean value false in scripts. `OP_0` is also used to initialize scripts.

`OP_0` is identical to `OP_FALSE` (`0X00`) and `OP_PUSHNUM_0`.

entries.title: OP_0NOTEQUAL - 0X92
entries.body: Checks whether the element at the top of the stack is different from zero. If the element is other than zero, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

entries.title: OP_1 - 0X51
entries.body:
Pushes the value `1` onto the stack. It is often used to represent the boolean value true in scripts.

`OP_1` is identical to `OP_TRUE` (`0X51`) and `OP_PUSHNUM_1`.

entries.title: OP_1ADD - 0X8B
entries.body: Adds `1` to the value at the top of the stack.

entries.title: OP_1NEGATE - 0X4F
entries.body: Pushes the value `-1` onto the stack. This opcode is used in scripts to represent the negative value `-1`.

entries.title: OP_1SUB - 0X8C
entries.body: Subtracts `1` from the value at the top of the stack.

entries.title: OP_2 TO OP_16 - 0X52 TO 0X60
entries.body:
The opcodes from `OP_2` through `OP_16` push the respective numeric values from 2 to 16 onto the stack. They are used to simplify scripts by allowing the insertion of small numeric values. This type of opcode is notably used in multisignature scripts. Here is an example of `scriptPubKey` for a 2/3 multisig: 

```text
OP_2
<Clé publique A>
<Clé publique B>
<Clé publique C>
OP_3
OP_CHECKMULTISIG
```

All of these opcodes are sometimes also named `OP_PUSHNUM_N`.

entries.title: OP_2DROP - 0XD6
entries.body: Removes the two elements at the top of the stack. In other words, `OP_2DROP` removes the top of the stack and the second element of the stack. This opcode is the equivalent of chaining two `OP_DROP`.

entries.title: OP_2DUP - 0X6E
entries.body:
Duplicates the two elements at the top of the stack, then places them at the top of the stack. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
```

`OP_2DUP` will produce: 

```text
A
B
A
B
C
D
```

entries.title: OP_2OVER - 0X70
entries.body:
Copies the two elements located at the fourth and third positions from the top of the stack, then places them at the top of the stack. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
```

`OP_2OVER` will produce:

```text
C
D
A
B
C
D
```

entries.title: OP_2ROT - 0X71
entries.body:
Moves the two items that are at the sixth and fifth places from the top of the stack to the top. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
E
F
```

`OP_2ROT` will produce:

```text
E
F
A
B
C
D
```

entries.title: OP_2SWAP - 0X72
entries.body:
Swaps the two items at the top of the stack with the two items located just below them. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
```

`OP_2SWAP` will produce:

```text
C
D
A
B
```

entries.title: OP_3DUP - 0X6F
entries.body:
Duplicates the three items at the top of the stack, then places them at the top of the stack. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
```

`OP_3DUP` will produce:

```text
A
B
C
A
B
C
D
```

entries.title: OP_ABS - 0X90
entries.body: Replaces the top item of the stack with its absolute value. This operation removes the sign of the item, turning any negative value into a positive one, without changing positive values.

entries.title: OP_ADD - 0X93
entries.body: Adds the two items at the top of the stack. It takes the two values at the top of the stack, adds them together and replaces them with the result.

entries.title: OP_BOOLAND - 0X9A
entries.body: Reproduces the behavior of a logical `AND` gate. It takes two values at the top of the stack and returns `1` only if both values are non-zero. Otherwise, it returns `0`.

entries.title: OP_BOOLOR - 0X9B
entries.body: Reproduces the behavior of a logical `OR` gate. It takes two values at the top of the stack and returns `1` if either one of the items or both are non-zero. Otherwise, it returns `0`.

entries.title: OP_CAT - 0X7E
OP_CHECKHASHVERIFY - CHV
entries.body: New opcode proposed in 2012 in BIP-0017 by Luke Dashjr, offering the same functionality as `OP_EVAL` or P2SH. It would have made it possible to hash the end of the `scriptSig`, compare the result with the top of the stack and make the transaction invalid if the two hashes did not match. This opcode was never implemented.

entries.title: OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY - 0XB1
OP_CHECKMULTISIG - 0XAE
entries.body: Verifies several signatures against several public keys. It takes as input a series of `N` public keys and `M` signatures, where `M` can be less than or equal to `N`. `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` checks whether at least `M` signatures match `M` of the `N` public keys. Note that, because of a historical *off-by-one* bug, an extra item is removed from the stack by `OP_CHECKMULTISIG`. This item is called the “*dummy element*”. To avoid an error in the `scriptSig`, a `OP_0` is therefore included, which is a useless item meant to satisfy the removal and work around the bug. Since BIP-0147 (introduced with SegWit in 2017), the useless item consumed because of the bug must be `OP_0` for the script to be valid, because it was a malleability vector. This opcode was removed in Tapscript.

entries.title: OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY - 0XAF
entries.body: Combines a `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and a `OP_VERIFY`. It takes several signatures and public keys to verify that `M` out of `N` signatures are valid, as `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` does. Then, like `OP_VERIFY`, if the verification fails, the script stops immediately with an error. If the verification succeeds, the script continues without pushing a value onto the stack. This opcode was removed in Tapscript.

entries.title: OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY - 0XB2
OP_CHECKSIG - 0XAC
entries.body: Verifies the validity of a signature against a given public key. It takes the two items at the top of the stack: the signature and the public key, and evaluates whether the signature is correct for the transaction hash and the specified public key. If the verification succeeds, it pushes the value `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise `0` (false). This opcode was modified in Tapscript in order to verify Schnorr signatures.

entries.title: OP_CHECKSIGADD - 0XBA
entries.body:
Pops the three values at the top of the stack: a `clé publique`, a `CScriptNum` `n` and a `signature`. If the signature is not the empty vector and is not valid, the script terminates with an error. If the signature is valid or is the empty vector (`OP_0`), two cases arise:
* If the signature is the empty vector: a `CScriptNum` with the value of `n` is pushed onto the stack and execution continues;
* If the signature is not the empty vector and remains valid: a `CScriptNum` with the value of `n + 1` is pushed onto the stack and execution continues.
In simple terms, `OP_CHECKSIGADD` performs an operation similar to `OP_CHECKSIG`, but instead of pushing true or false onto the stack, it adds `1` to the second value from the top of the stack if the signature is valid, or leaves that value unchanged if the signature is the empty vector. `OP_CHECKSIGADD` makes it possible to create the same multisig policies in Tapscript as with `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` but in a batch-verifiable way, that is, it removes the search process in the verification of a traditional multisig and therefore speeds up verification while reducing the operational load on nodes' CPUs. This opcode was added in Tapscript solely for the needs of Taproot.

entries.title: OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK - 0XCC
entries.body:
Opcode `0xcc` proposed in BIP-0348 for Tapscript, as a replacement for `OP_SUCCESS204`. Unlike `OP_CHECKSIG`, which verifies a signature over a hash derived from the current transaction, `OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK` makes it possible to verify a Schnorr signature over an arbitrary message provided directly on the stack.

Execution begins by reading three items from the top of the stack: the public key (top), the message (second position) and the signature (third position). These three items are then removed from the stack. If the public key is empty, the script fails immediately. If it is 32 bytes long, it is interpreted as a BIP-0340 key: a non-empty signature is then validated according to the Schnorr scheme against this key and the message, and any invalid signature causes the script to stop. An empty signature pushes an empty vector onto the stack and execution continues normally. A valid signature pushes the value `0x01`. Keys of a length other than 0 and 32 bytes are treated as unknown types, and their verification always succeeds in order to allow for future extensions.

Each verification with a non-empty signature is counted in the sigops budget defined by BIP-0342. This ability to authenticate arbitrary data would open up possibilities such as transaction introspection, delegation of spending rights and the construction of Lightning Symmetry channels. This proposal is for the moment still a draft, and therefore not implemented on Bitcoin.

entries.title: OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY - 0XAD
entries.body: Performs the same operation as `OP_CHECKSIG`, but if the signature verification fails, the script stops immediately with an error and the transaction is therefore invalid. If the verification succeeds, the script continues without pushing a `1` (true) value onto the stack. To sum up, `OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY` performs the `OP_CHECKSIG` operation followed by `OP_VERIFY`. This opcode was modified in Tapscript in order to verify Schnorr signatures.

entries.title: OP_CHECKTEMPLATEVERIFY - 0XB3
entries.body:
Opcode `0xb3` proposed in BIP-0119, as a replacement for `OP_NOP4`. It requires the spending transaction to match a predefined template exactly, which makes it a non-recursive covenant mechanism.

The opcode reads the item at the top of the stack without removing it. If this item is 32 bytes long, it is compared to the `DefaultCheckTemplateVerifyHash` computed from the current transaction and the index of the input being executed. This hash is the `SHA256` of the serialized concatenation of: the transaction version, the locktime, the hash of the scriptSigs (if they are non-empty), the number of inputs, the hash of the sequences, the number of outputs, the hash of the outputs and the index of the current input. If the two values do not match, the script fails. If the item is not 32 bytes long, the opcode behaves like a `OP_NOP` in order to allow for future extensions.

By constraining almost all of the fields of the spending transaction, CTV makes it possible to specify the exact outputs in advance without resorting to signatures or ephemeral keys. This property opens the way to applications such as payment trees for congestion control, *vaults*, joinpools or improving the efficiency of DLCs. This proposal is for the moment still a draft.

entries.title: OP_CODESEPARATOR - 0XAB
entries.body: Modifies the current output script, indicating that only the operations that follow this opcode will be taken into account in the verification of the signatures of the corresponding inputs. This makes it possible to segment a complex script into several parts, where each segment can be signed independently.

entries.title: OP_DEPTH - 0X74
entries.body: Pushes the number of items in the stack onto the stack itself. If the stack contains `N` items, `OP_DEPTH` will add the number `N` as a new item at the top of the stack.

entries.title: OP_DROP - 0X75
entries.body: Removes the item at the top of the stack. `OP_DROP` makes it possible to discard data that has become useless during the execution of the script.

entries.title: OP_DUP - 0X76
entries.body: Duplicates the top of the stack. The item at the top of the stack is thus copied and the copy is placed at the top of the stack.

entries.title: OP_ELSE - 0X67
entries.body: Modifies the execution flow in a conditional script: it indicates that the operations that follow it must be executed if the previous condition specified by an `OP_IF` or an `OP_NOTIF` is not met.

entries.title: OP_ENDIF - 0X68
entries.body: Marks the end of a conditional control structure initiated by an `OP_IF` or an `OP_NOTIF`, normally followed by one or more `OP_ELSE`. It indicates that script execution must continue beyond the conditional structure, regardless of which branch was executed. In other words, `OP_ENDIF` delimits the end of conditional blocks in scripts.

entries.title: OP_EQUAL - 0X87
entries.body: Compares the two topmost values of the stack and pushes `1` onto the stack if they are equal, otherwise pushes `0`. `OP_EQUAL` makes it possible to check the equality of data in a script.

entries.title: OP_EQUALVERIFY - 0X88
entries.body: Combines the functions of `OP_EQUAL` and `OP_VERIFY`. It first checks the equality of the two upper values of the stack, then requires the result to be non-zero, failing which the transaction is invalid. `OP_EQUALVERIFY` is notably used in address verification scripts.

entries.title: OP_EVAL
entries.body: Opcode proposed by Gavin Andresen in 2011. It takes the script located at the top of the stack, executes it as if it were part of the `scriptPubKey`, and places its result on the stack. `OP_EVAL` was abandoned because of concerns about the complexity of this opcode, which would eventually be superseded by P2SH.

entries.title: OP_FALSE - 0X00
entries.body: Identical to `OP_0`.

entries.title: OP_FROMALTSTACK - 0X6C
entries.body: Removes the top of the alternate stack (*alt stack*) and places it on top of the main stack (*main stack*). This opcode is used to retrieve data temporarily stored on the alternate stack. To put it simply, it is the inverse operation of `OP_TOALTSTACK`.

entries.title: OP_GREATERTHAN - 0XA0
entries.body: Compares the two items at the top of the stack and checks whether the first item is greater than the second. If the first item is greater than the second, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

entries.title: OP_GREATERTHANOREQUAL - 0XA2
entries.body: Compares the two items at the top of the stack and checks whether the second item is greater than or equal to the first. If the second item is greater than or equal to the first, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

entries.title: OP_HASH160 - 0XA9
entries.body: Takes the item at the top of the stack and replaces it with its hash, using the `SHA256` and then `RIPEMD160` functions in succession. This two-step process generates a 160-bit digest.

entries.title: OP_HASH256 - 0XAA
entries.body: Takes the item at the top of the stack and replaces it with its hash, using the `SHA256` function twice. The input is hashed a first time with `SHA256` and the digest is hashed a second time with `SHA256`. This two-step process generates a 256-bit digest.

entries.title: OP_IF - 0X63
entries.body:
Executes the following portion of the script if the value at the top of the stack is non-zero (true). If the value is zero (false), these operations are skipped, going directly to those after `OP_ELSE`, if present. `OP_IF` makes it possible to start a conditional control structure in a script. It determines the control flow in a script based on a condition provided at the time the transaction is executed. `OP_IF` is used with `OP_ELSE` and `OP_ENDIF` in the following way: 

```text
<condition>
OP_IF
<opérations si la condition est vraie>
OP_ELSE
<opérations si la condition est fausse>
OP_ENDIF
```

entries.title: OP_IFDUP - 0X73
entries.body: Duplicates the top of the stack if it is non-zero. If the value at the top of the stack is true (that is, non-zero), this value is duplicated on the stack; otherwise, the stack remains unchanged.

entries.title: OP_INTERNALKEY - 0XCB
entries.body: Opcode proposed in BIP-0349 to be added to Tapscript (`0xcb`), which pushes the Taproot internal key (*internal key*) onto the stack. In practice, when a script in a Taproot leaf needs to know the public key that was used to construct the output, it can call `OP_INTERNALKEY` instead of having to hardcode this key in the script. The result is the 32-byte *x-only* representation of the internal key.

entries.title: OP_LESSTHAN - 0X9F
entries.body: Compares the top two elements of the stack and checks whether the second element is less than the first. If the second element is less than the first, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

entries.title: OP_LESSTHANOREQUAL - 0XA1
entries.body: Compares the top two elements of the stack and checks whether the second element is less than or equal to the first. If the second element is less than or equal to the first, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

entries.title: OP_MAX - 0XA4
entries.body: Selects the larger of the top two elements of the stack and pushes it onto the stack. This operation keeps only the larger of the two top values.

entries.title: OP_MIN - 0XA3
entries.body: Selects the smaller of the top two elements of the stack and pushes it onto the stack. This operation keeps only the smaller of the two top values.

entries.title: OP_NEGATE - 0X8F
entries.body: Reverses the sign of the top element of the stack. If the value is positive, it becomes negative, and vice versa.

entries.title: OP_NIP - 0X77
entries.body: Removes the element located just below the top of the stack (the second from the top).

entries.title: OP_NOP - 0X61
entries.body:
Has no effect on the stack or the script state. It performs no movement, no verification, and no modification. It simply does nothing, unless it has been decided otherwise through a soft fork. Indeed, since their modification by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2010, the `OP_NOP` (`OP_NOP1` (`0XB0`) through `OP_NOP10` (`0XB9`)) commands have been used to add new opcodes as soft forks. 

Thus, `OP_NOP2` (`0XB1`) and `OP_NOP3` (`0XB2`) have already been used to implement `OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY` and `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY` respectively. They are used in combination with `OP_DROP` in order to remove the associated time values from the stack, and thus be able to continue script execution, whether the node is up to date or not. The `OP_NOP` therefore make it possible to insert a breakpoint in a script to check additional conditions that already exist or that could be added with future soft forks. Since Tapscript, the use of `OP_NOP` has been replaced by the use of `OP_SUCCESS`, which is more efficient.

entries.title: OP_NOT - 0X91
entries.body: Inverts the boolean value at the top of the stack: if this value is non-zero, the operator replaces it with 0, otherwise with 1.

entries.title: OP_NOTIF - 0X64
entries.body: Works in the opposite way to `OP_IF`, executing the following portion of the script if the value at the top of the stack is zero (false).

entries.title: OP_NUMEQUAL - 0X9C
entries.body: Compares the top two elements of the stack to check whether they are numerically equal. If the values are equal, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

entries.title: OP_NUMEQUALVERIFY - 0X9D
entries.body: Combines the `OP_NUMEQUAL` and `OP_VERIFY` operations. It numerically compares the top two elements of the stack. If the values are equal, `OP_NUMEQUALVERIFY` removes the true result from the stack and script execution continues. If the values are not equal, the result is false and the script fails immediately.

entries.title: OP_NUMNOTEQUAL - 0X9E
entries.body: Compares the top two elements of the stack to check whether they are numerically not equal. If the values are not equal, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false). It is the inverse of `OP_NUMEQUAL`.

entries.title: OP_OVER - 0X78
entries.body: Duplicates the second element from the top of the stack and places it on the top of the stack.

entries.title: OP_PICK - 0X79
entries.body: Duplicates an element of the stack and places it at the top of the stack, based on the depth specified by the value at the top of the stack before the operation. For example, if the value at the top of the stack is `4`, `OP_PICK` will duplicate the fifth element of the stack from the top (indexing starts at `0`), and it will place this copy at the top.

entries.title: OP_PUSHDATA1 - 0X4C
entries.body: Pushes a certain amount of data onto the stack. It is followed by one byte that indicates the length of the data to push (up to 255 bytes). This opcode is used to include variable-size data in scripts.

entries.title: OP_PUSHDATA2 - 0X4D
entries.body: Makes it possible to push a large amount of data onto the stack. It is followed by two bytes (little-endian) that specify the length of the data to push (up to 65,535 bytes). It is used to insert larger data into scripts.

entries.title: OP_PUSHDATA4 - 0X4E
entries.body: Makes it possible to push a very large amount of data onto the stack. It is followed by four bytes (little-endian) that indicate the length of the data to push (up to approximately 4.3 GB). This opcode is used to insert very large data into scripts, although its use is extremely rare because of the practical limitations on transaction size.

entries.title: OP_RETURN - 0X6A
entries.body: Marks a script as invalid, which makes the output containing it provably unspendable. Nodes on the network can therefore remove this output from their UTXO set. `OP_RETURN` is often used to inscribe arbitrary data in the blockchain.

entries.title: OP_RIPEMD160 - 0XA6
entries.body: Takes the element at the top of the stack and replaces it with its hash using the `RIPEMD160` function.

entries.title: OP_ROLL - 0X7A
entries.body: Moves an element of the stack to the top of the stack, based on the depth specified by the value at the top of the stack before the operation. For example, if the value at the top of the stack is `4`, `OP_ROLL` will select the fifth element of the stack from the top (indexing starts at `0`), and it will move this value to the top. `OP_ROLL` plays the same role as `OP_PICK`, except that it removes the element from its original position.

entries.title: OP_ROT - 0X7B
entries.body: Moves the third element from the top of the stack to the top of the stack. The two elements that were above it are pushed below it, keeping their relative order.

entries.title: OP_SHA1 - 0XA7
entries.body: Takes the element at the top of the stack and replaces it with its hash using the `SHA1` function. The use of this function is nowadays discouraged in a secure setting.

entries.title: OP_SHA256 - 0XA8
entries.body: Takes the element at the top of the stack and replaces it with its hash using the `SHA256` function.

entries.title: OP_SIZE - 0X82
entries.body: Measures the size in number of bytes of the element at the top of the stack and returns this size to the top of the stack, without modifying the analyzed element itself.

entries.title: OP_SUB - 0X94
entries.body: Subtracts the top two elements of the stack. It takes the two values at the top of the stack, subtracts them, and replaces them with the result.

entries.title: OP_SUCCESS
entries.body:
The `OP_SUCCESS` represent a series of opcodes that were disabled in the past and are now reserved for future use in Tapscript. Their ultimate purpose is to facilitate upgrades and extensions of the script language, by allowing the introduction of new features via soft forks. When one of these opcodes is encountered in a script, it causes the immediate and unconditional success of the entire script, regardless of the data or conditions present. Execution does not continue: the script is directly considered valid. 

Thus, when a new opcode is added to an `OP_SUCCESS`, this necessarily represents the addition of a rule that is more restrictive than the previous rule. Up-to-date nodes can then verify compliance with this rule, and nodes that are not up to date will not reject the associated transactions and the blocks that include them, because the `OP_SUCCESS` validates this part of the script. There is therefore no hard fork. 

In comparison, the `OP_NOP` (*No Operation*) also serve as placeholders in the script, but they have no effect on script execution. When a `OP_NOP` is encountered, the script simply continues without modifying the state of the stack or the course of the script. The key difference therefore lies in their impact on execution: `OP_SUCCESS` causes the immediate success of the entire script, whereas `OP_NOP` is neutral, and affects neither the stack nor the flow of the script. These opcodes are designated by `OP_SUCCESSN` where `N` is a number that makes it possible to differentiate the `OP_SUCCESS`.

entries.title: OP_SWAP - 0X7C
entries.body: Swaps the top two elements of the stack. The element that was at the top is moved to second position, and the element that was in second position is placed at the top of the stack.

entries.title: OP_TOALTSTACK - 0X6B
entries.body: Takes the top of the main stack (*main stack*) and moves it to the alternate stack (*alt stack*). This opcode makes it possible to temporarily store data aside for later use in the script. The moved element is therefore removed from the main stack. `OP_FROMALTSTACK` will then be used to put it back on the top of the main stack.

entries.title: OP_TRUE - 0X51
entries.body: Identical to `OP_1`. It pushes the value `1` onto the stack. It is often used to represent the boolean value true in scripts.

entries.title: OP_TUCK - 0X7D
entries.body:
Copies the element at the top of the stack and inserts it between the second element and the third element of the stack. For example, if the stack is:

```text
A
B
C
D
```

`OP_TUCK` will duplicate the top `A` and place it in third position. The resulting stack will be:

```text
A
B
A
C
D
```

entries.title: OP_TXHASH - 0XBD
entries.body:
Opcode `0xbd` proposed in BIP-0346 for Tapscript, replacing `OP_SUCCESS189`. It provides a general-purpose transaction introspection mechanism that produces a configurable hash from certain fields of the spending transaction.

The opcode removes from the top of the stack an element called `TxFieldSelector`, a serialized structure that determines which transaction fields must be included in the hash. This selector makes it possible to target, as desired: global fields (version, locktime, current input index), per-input fields (prevouts, sequences, scriptSigs, values and scriptPubkeys of the spent UTXOs, Taproot annexes) and per-output fields (scriptPubkeys, values). It also offers several modes for selecting inputs and outputs: all, only the one at the current index, the first N, or a set of individual indices. After validating the selector, the opcode pushes onto the stack the 32-byte `SHA256` hash computed from the selected fields.

With an empty `TxFieldSelector`, `OP_TXHASH` produces a hash semantically equivalent to that of `OP_CHECKTEMPLATEVERIFY`, which makes it a strict generalization of BIP-0119. Combined with `OP_CHECKSIGFROMSTACK`, it would make it possible to build arbitrary signature hashes and to emulate `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` as well as other signature modes. This proposal is for the moment still a draft.

entries.title: OP_VAULT - 0XBB
entries.body:
Opcode `0xbb` proposed in BIP-0345 for Tapscript, replacing `OP_SUCCESS187`. It constitutes the mechanism of a specialized covenant vault system, which makes it possible to impose a configurable delay before any spend, with the possibility of recovery in case of compromise.

The opcode consumes several elements from the stack (from the top down): a `<leaf-update-script-body>` that contains the body of the replacement script, a `<push-count>` that indicates the number of additional data elements, the corresponding data elements, a `<trigger-vout-idx>` that designates the index of the trigger output, a `<revault-vout-idx>` that designates the index of an optional “revault” output (`-1` if absent), and a `<revault-amount>` that specifies the amount in satoshis to place back into the vault. From these elements, the opcode builds a replacement script by prefixing the `<leaf-update-script-body>` with the provided data, then verifies that the trigger output has a taptree identical to that of the current input, except for the leaf being executed, which is replaced by this new script. This Taproot leaf substitution preserves all the other leaves, including the recovery path via `OP_VAULT_RECOVER` (`0xbc`).

The opcode records deferred checks to ensure that the value of the input is fully carried over between the trigger output and the possible “revault” output. This mechanism makes it possible to group several vault inputs in a single transaction. On success, the value `0x01` is pushed onto the stack. BIP-0345 has been closed and replaced by BIP-0443 (`OP_CHECKCONTRACTVERIFY`), which is more general-purpose.

entries.title: OP_VER - 0X62
entries.body: Used to push the protocol version onto the stack. This opcode was disabled, because had it been used, every update would have led to a hard fork. BIP-0342 changed this opcode into `OP_SUCCESS`.

entries.title: OP_VERIFY - 0X69
entries.body: Requires that the value at the top of the stack be non-zero (true). The transaction is invalid if this is not the case. `OP_VERIFY` is used to confirm script conditions.

entries.title: OP_WITHIN - 0XA5
entries.body: Checks whether the first element at the top of the stack lies within the range defined by the second and third top elements. In other words, `OP_WITHIN` checks whether the first element is greater than or equal to the second and less than the third. If this condition is true, it pushes `1` (true) onto the stack, otherwise, it pushes `0` (false).

entries.title: OPCODES
entries.body: The set of commands used in Bitcoin's Script system. Script is a stack-based programming language used to establish spending conditions, and therefore, indirectly, to secure bitcoins. The instructions used in the Script language are called "opcodes". They are logical operators and commands for manipulating stacks (*stacks*). These specific instructions are executed by the network's nodes when validating a transaction. Script is a non-Turing-complete language. It can be categorized as a mid-level language (almost low-level) inspired by Forth.

entries.title: OPENDIME
entries.body: A single-use USB device made by Coinkite, designed as a bearer asset for bitcoins. The Opendime generates a private key internally the first time it is used. This key is known to no one. Bitcoins can then be sent to the associated address. To spend the bitcoins secured by this key, the device must be physically unsealed by inserting a pin into a hole provided for that purpose on the circuit board. The private key is then revealed in WIF format and the user can spend the associated funds. As long as the device remains sealed, it can be passed from hand to hand without generating an on-chain transaction. The physical seal makes it possible to verify with certainty, during an exchange, that the private key is not known to the payer, simply by inspecting the device.

entries.title: OPENNODE
entries.body: A bitcoin payment processing platform. OpenNode provides an API that allows merchants and developers to accept bitcoin payments, both on the main chain and via the Lightning Network. The platform offers checkout pages, billing links and integration tools. Merchants using this service can choose to receive their funds in bitcoin or directly in fiat currency in their bank account. Note that OpenNode is not a *self-custody* payment terminal, unlike BTCPayServer for example.

entries.title: OPENSATS
entries.body: A non-profit organization founded in 2021, dedicated to funding free and *open source* projects related to Bitcoin. Structured as a charitable association in the United States, OpenSats distributes grants to developers and projects that contribute to the Bitcoin ecosystem and its adjacent technologies.

entries.title: OPENTIMESTAMPS
entries.body: A decentralized *open source* timestamping protocol, developed by Peter Todd. OpenTimestamps uses the Bitcoin blockchain to prove the existence of a document or piece of data at a precise point in time. The protocol computes a cryptographic fingerprint (*hash*) of the file to be timestamped, then anchors this fingerprint in a Bitcoin transaction by means of a Merkle tree. The result is a verifiable and tamper-proof proof attesting that the data existed at the moment the corresponding Bitcoin block was mined. This system is useful for intellectual property, contracts, legal evidence or any situation that requires proof of time.

entries.title: ORACLE
entries.body: A third-party source of information that provides real-world data that can be interpreted on Bitcoin. Oracles allow smart contracts, such as DLCs, to execute contractual conditions based on external events. In general, they provide a specific signature that corresponds to the outcome of an event. This signature is then used to complete and make valid an execution transaction that sends the bitcoins to the party that is supposed to receive them according to the terms of the smart contract.

entries.title: ORDINAL NUMBER
entries.body: Within the Ordinals protocol, it is a unique identifier assigned to each sat according to its mining order. These numbers make these sats non-fungible under the Ordinals protocol, and therefore make it possible to track and transfer these specific sats.

entries.title: ORDINALS THEORY
entries.body: A protocol external to Bitcoin that assigns serial numbers to sats (the smallest unit of bitcoin), which makes it possible to trace them individually and transfer them via Bitcoin transactions. According to Ordinals theory, each sat is numbered according to the order in which it was mined and is transferred on a FIFO (*First-In-First-Out*) basis. The goal of this theory is to make sats non-fungible according to their interpretation within the Ordinals protocol, in order to associate information with them such as images (NFTs) called "inscriptions".

entries.title: ORPHAN BLOCK
entries.body:
Theoretically, an orphan block designates a valid block received by a node that has not yet acquired the parent block, that is to say the previous one in the chain. This block, although valid, remains locally isolated as an orphan.

However, in common usage, the expression "orphan block" often refers to a block without a child: a valid block, but not retained in Bitcoin's main chain. It occurs when two miners find a valid block at the same chain height within a short period of time and broadcast it on the network. The nodes end up choosing a single block to include in the chain, according to the principle of the chain with the most accumulated work, making the other one an "orphan".

![Fork after block 144: 145-B is followed by block 146 and 145-A remains without a child, described as orphaned.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/o/orphelin/assets/image-1.png)

*Personally, I prefer to use the term "orphan block" to speak of a block without a parent and the term "stale block" (stale block) to designate a block that has no child. I find this more logical and understandable, although a majority of bitcoiners do not follow this usage.*

entries.title: OSINT
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Open Source Intelligence*". OSINT refers to the collection and analysis of publicly available information from sources accessible to everyone. These sources can include websites, forums, social networks, public databases, academic publications, government documents, etc. The main goal of OSINT is to transform raw data into actionable information, by identifying trends, correlations and investigative leads.

In the context of Bitcoin, OSINT can be used to support a chain analysis in order to trace funds, notably to identify an entry point, that is to say a link between on-chain activity and a form of identity belonging to a real entity. For example, if you publish your receiving address on Twitter under your name, an analyst could find it and associate it with your identity.

![OSINT link: a tweet by Loïc Morel publishing their address bc1q...acd makes it possible to link this address cluster to their identity.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/o/osint/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: OUTBOUND CAPACITY
entries.body: Designates the maximum amount of bitcoins that a node can send through a specific channel on the Lightning Network. It depends on the funds the node committed to the channel when opening it, or that it received during a Lightning payment or routing.

entries.title: OUTPOINT
entries.body:
A unique reference to a transaction output (*output*). It consists of two elements:
* `txid`: the identifier of the transaction that created the output;
* `vout`: the index of the output in the transaction.

The combination of these two elements makes it possible to precisely identify a transaction output. For example, if a transaction has a `txid` of `abc...123` and the output index is `0`, the outpoint will be written:

```text
abc...123:0
```

The outpoint is used in the inputs (`vin`) of a new transaction to indicate which UTXO is being spent.

*The term "outpoint" is often used as a synonym for "UTXO".*

entries.title: OUTPUT
entries.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, an output within a transaction refers to the _Unspent Transaction Outputs_ (UTXOs) that are created as destination funds for the payment. More precisely, it is a mechanism by which a transaction distributes funds. A transaction takes UTXOs, that is to say pieces of bitcoins, as "inputs" and creates new UTXOs as "outputs". These outputs stipulate a certain amount of bitcoins, often assigned to a specific address, as well as the conditions under which these funds can later be spent.

The role of the Bitcoin transaction is therefore to consume UTXOs as inputs, and to create new UTXOs as outputs. The difference between the two corresponds to the transaction fees, which can be collected by the winning miner of the block. A UTXO is, in essence, the output of a previous transaction that has not yet been spent. Transaction outputs are therefore the creations of new UTXOs which will, in turn, potentially be used as inputs in future transactions.

From a broader perspective, in computer science, the term "output" generally designates the data resulting from a function, an algorithm, or a system. For example, when data is passed into a cryptographic hash function, this information is called "input", and the result is called "output".

entries.title: OUTPUT LINKING
entries.body: A synonym sometimes used to refer to address reuse. *Output linking* refers to the practice of using the same receiving address to lock several UTXOs, sometimes within several different transactions. Bitcoins are generally locked using a cryptographic key pair that corresponds to a unique address. Since the blockchain is public, it is easy to see which addresses are associated with how many bitcoins. In the case of reuse of the same address for several payments, one can imagine that all the associated UTXOs belong to the same entity. Address reuse therefore poses a problem for the user's privacy. It makes it possible to make deterministic links between several transactions and several UTXOs, as well as to perpetuate *on-chain* fund tracing.

entries.title: OUTPUT SCRIPT DESCRIPTORS
entries.body:
Output script descriptors, or simply descriptors, are structured expressions that fully describe an output script (`scriptPubKey`) and provide all the information needed to track transactions to or from a particular script. These descriptors make key management easier in HD wallets thanks to a standard description of the structure and the types of addresses used.

The main value of descriptors lies in their ability to encapsulate all the information essential to restoring a wallet in a single string of characters (in addition to the recovery phrase). By backing up a descriptor with the corresponding mnemonic phrases, it is possible to restore not only the private keys, but also the precise structure of the wallet and the associated script parameters. Indeed, recovering a wallet requires not only knowledge of the initial seed, but also the specific indexes for the derivation of the child key pairs, as well as the `xpub` of each factor in the case of a multisig wallet. In the past, it was assumed that this information was implicitly known to everyone. However, with the diversification of scripts and the emergence of more complex configurations, this information could become difficult to extrapolate, thus turning this data into private information that is hard to brute-force. Using descriptors greatly simplifies the process: it is enough to know the recovery phrase or phrases and the corresponding descriptor to restore everything reliably and securely.

A descriptor is made up of several elements:
* Script functions such as `pk` (Pay-to-PubKey), `pkh` (Pay-to-PubKey-Hash), `wpkh` (Pay-to-Witness-PubKey-Hash), `sh` (Pay-to-Script-Hash), `wsh` (Pay-to-Witness-Script-Hash), `tr` (Pay-to-Taproot), `multi` (Multisignature) and `sortedmulti` (Multisignature with sorted keys);
* Derivation paths, for example `[d34db33f/44h/0h/0h]` which indicates a derived path and a specific master key fingerprint;
* Keys in various formats such as public keys in hexadecimal or extended public keys (`xpub`);
* A checksum, preceded by a hash sign, to verify the integrity of the descriptor.

For example, a descriptor for a P2WPKH wallet might look like:

```text
wpkh([cdeab12f/84h/0h/0h]xpub6CUGRUonZSQ4TWtTMmzXdrXDtyPWKiKbERr4d5qkSmh5h17C1TjvMt7DJ9Qve4dRxm91CDv6cNfKsq2mK1rMsJKhtRUPZz7MQtp3y6atC1U/<0;1>/*)#jy0l7nr4
```

In this descriptor, the derivation function `wpkh` indicates a Pay-to-Witness-Public-Key-Hash script type. It is followed by the derivation path which contains:
* `cdeab12f`: the master key fingerprint;
* `84h`: which means the use of a BIP-0084 purpose, intended for SegWit v0 addresses;
* `0h`: which indicates that it is a BTC currency on the mainnet;
* `0h`: which refers to the specific account number used in the wallet.

The descriptor also includes the extended public key used on this wallet: 

```text
xpub6CUGRUonZSQ4TWtTMmzXdrXDtyPWKiKbERr4d5qkSmh5h17C1TjvMt7DJ9Qve4dRxm91CDv6cNfKsq2mK1rMsJKhtRUPZz7MQtp3y6atC1U
```

Next, the notation `/<0;1>/*` specifies that the descriptor can generate addresses from the external chain (`0`) and internal chain (`1`), with a wildcard (`*`) allowing the sequential derivation of several addresses in a configurable manner, similar to the management of a "gap limit" on conventional wallet software.

Finally, `#jy0l7nr4` represents the checksum used to verify the integrity of the descriptor.

entries.title: OVERCLOCKING
entries.body: A practice that consists of increasing the operating frequency of the ASIC chips used for mining beyond their nominal specifications. This makes it possible to produce more hashrate and to increase the chances of finding a block. However, this practice also increases the machines' electricity consumption, and therefore generates more heat, which can lead to premature wear of the components and require improved cooling systems, such as immersion cooling.

entries.title: OVERT ASICBOOST
entries.body: The open and transparent version of AsicBoost. AsicBoost is an algorithmic optimization technique used in Bitcoin mining. Miners using the Overt version manipulate the `nVersion` field of the candidate block and use this modification as an additional nonce. This modification of the `nVersion` field makes it possible to change the data of the first SHA256 chunk of the header, and thus to reuse the intermediate result (*midstate*) of this first chunk for all the iterations of the `Nonce`, which reduces the necessary calculations. This version is publicly detectable and does not hide its modifications from the rest of the network, unlike the Covert version of AsicBoost.

entries.title: OWNED STATE
entries.body: Within the RGB protocol, the Owned State designates the portion of the Contract State encapsulated in an Assignment and explicitly associated with a particular holder by means of a Single-use Seal pointing to a UTXO. This component represents, for example, a digital asset or a specific contractual right assigned to an individual. By isolating the state linked to each holder, the Owned State guarantees precise and secure management of ownership within RGB smart contracts.

entries.title: OWNERSHIP
entries.body: Within the RGB protocol, the term Ownership designates the property which, through the Seal Definition pointing to a Bitcoin UTXO, defines who can modify the state of a contract. When an Owned State is associated with a UTXO, the owner of the latter holds the right, in accordance with the rules of the contract, to transfer or to evolve the corresponding state.

entries.title: OXT
entries.body:
An exploratory analysis tool for the Bitcoin blockchain, created by LaurentMT and then acquired by Samourai Wallet. OXT offered advanced chain exploration and visualization features, with a particular focus on the study of transaction privacy.

The platform made it possible to visualize transaction graphs, to compute privacy metrics such as the Boltzmann score and to identify usage *patterns* (*coinjoins*, consolidations, etc.). It thus served to understand and audit the level of privacy offered by a transaction or a set of transactions.

The service, formerly accessible for free at oxt.me, has been offline since April 2024, following the legal proceedings brought against the founders of Samourai Wallet.
